title: Sweet speech
hook: speak sweetly, as Asa di Var asks
tomorrow: a rumor about a friend hits the group chat. does Simran pass it on?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thieves, reviewed: five of them, living in the house of the self, quieter when the light is on. The house is safer. Now, the last words at the door.
screen: `THE HOUSE IS SAFER.` → `THE LAST WORDS AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: At the door, Bebe hugs her son, then Bhua Kiran, then Simran last and longest. Simran braces for a speech about the thieves. Instead Bebe holds her face in both hands and says, in Punjabi, the softest thing: you were good medicine, putt. Then she gets in the car, rolls the window down, and waves until the car turns the corner. Simran stands on the porch a long time. All those days of breathing, saying sorry and putting things back on the shelf, and what she'll remember is one sentence.
screen: `THE LAST AND LONGEST HUG.` → `YOU WERE GOOD MEDICINE.` → `ONE SENTENCE TO REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak has a line about that, in Asa di Var, on ang 473, in paraphrase: speak tasteless, harsh words, and body and mind turn tasteless too. Speech isn't only what comes out; it shapes the one who speaks. On ang 470 he puts sweetness at the center: sweetness and humility, says Nanak, are the essence of every virtue. Sweet speech isn't flattery, and it isn't fake politeness. Bebe's sentence was true. It was just true in the kindest way. She could have said: stop yelling, stop scrolling, stop clutching. All of that was true too. She chose the sentence that would still be warm in a year. And that's the thread through these two weeks. Every family, welcomed. A full place. Seva at home. Breathe first; softly at home; enough; free hands. Love, not clutch, when Bebe chose to go home. Gifts, not trophies. No holier than others. See the soul. The medicine. The house is safer. In the end, most of it showed up as words: a sorry on the couch, a text to Bhua Kiran, a message that took the photos down, a list of names on the phone. The thieves speak harshly; the virtues speak sweetly. Bebe knew it. Here's the line to repeat tonight: a harsh word makes a harsh speaker, and a sweet one makes a sweet one.
screen: `ANG 473: HARSH WORDS, HARSH MIND.` · `ANG 470: SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · `TRUE, IN THE KINDEST WAY.` · `TWO WEEKS, SPOKEN SWEETLY.` · then, large: `SWEET WORDS.`

segments.voice: Think of one person you'll see or talk to soon. Find one true, kind sentence you could say to them, then say it out loud once, quietly, to hear how it sounds in your own voice. Let it rest on your tongue as you breathe.
Sweet speech. Mithat: sweetness, true words said in the kindest way, which shape the one who speaks them.
Sweet words: true, kind, and good for the speaker too. A new week starts tomorrow.

howItsDone: Asa di Var is sung in many gurdwaras in the early morning, and its lines on sweet, humble speech are often quoted in Sikh homes as a guide for how to talk.

fork.setup: your friend's presentation went badly, and she asks what you honestly thought. what fits today's line?
options: one true thing that went well, and one true thing to fix, gently.
tell her it was perfect, so she doesn't feel bad.
list every problem, since honesty is what she asked for.
fork.reveal: sweet speech isn't flattery and isn't bluntness: it's true, said in the kindest way, like Bebe's sentence at the door.

chat.says: bebe said i was 'good medicine.' why did that hit harder than any speech?
options: it was true and kind at once. sweet words shape the speaker and the hearer.
because flattery always feels good, even when it isn't really true.
because she finally stopped correcting me about everything.
chat.meaning: Sweet speech is truth said kindly; Asa di Var says words shape the one who speaks them (ang 473) as well as the hearer.

Asa di Var.meaning: a ballad in Rag Asa by Guru Nanak, in the Guru Granth Sahib

putt.meaning: Punjabi for child; a term of affection
